Marcus took a year off, got deeply AI-pilled, learned Cursor, and is now "lightly technical — knows what a database migration is." He ships faster than almost anyone on the engineering team because he combines sharp product sense with AI-augmented execution. "We never could have hired him to do this job even a year ago. But the coding models have gotten good enough." Designers are the second group. Full-stack designers who can build visually distinct, high-quality interactions — precisely what vibe coding produces least well — are suddenly empowered to ship their own pull requests instead of handing off specifications. "They can build stuff that looks so different, and now they don't need to hand it off. They just make pull requests." The general principle Shipper offers is that models "make yesterday's human competence cheap." Anything that has already been done — a landing page, a tweet, a data analysis — can be replicated by a model instantly and universally. That commoditization is the engine of progress, but it also means that the default output of any model is slop. Value accrues to humans who can use the model's output as raw material for something new, unique, or situationally specific. > "Structurally, because of the way the models work and the financial incentives of model companies to make them compliant and aligned, models are always going to be trailing behind the people who take them and make new expertise. That stuff will get incorporated into the models, but it will create room for humans to push further ahead." The practical advice is simple: ride the models. Try every new release on your own problems. Turn over rocks: "It couldn't do this last time — can it do it now?" Shipper emphasizes that the edge of AI is not in San Francisco, where models are built, but wherever a model meets a real human doing something specific. "The people in San Francisco don't know everything about how to use it. They need to see how other people use it. When a new model comes out, you get to be one of the first people in the world to discover what it might be useful for." ## Cross-Theme Synthesis Four threads connect every prediction in this episode. **First**, the limiting factor in AI adoption is not model capability — it is human attention. Every autonomous system requires a human steward, and that creates new work rather than eliminating it. **Second**, the work surface is shifting decisively from standalone apps to agent-centered environments with embedded browsers, which will reshape SaaS architecture, pricing, and go-to-market. **Third**, the winners are not the most technical — they are the most curious and the most willing to apply models to their own problems, whether they are PMs, designers, or data scientists. **Fourth**, the horizon is not a job apocalypse but a reorganization: more PRs, more reviewing, more forward-deployed engineers, more internal writing by agents, and a permanent premium on human judgment about what should exist and what should be deleted. The most important unresolved question is whether the super-agent-per-company model gives way to personal agents faster than Shipper expects, or whether the maintenance burden remains prohibitive. The answer will determine not only how companies organize their engineering teams but also whether the balance of power in software shifts toward platform providers (like the companies that run Codex and Co-work) or toward the organizations that deploy them. AI agents and workCodex vs Claude CodeSaaS apocalypse debateAI job apocalypse mythPMs and designers thriveCLI era endingAgents need humansWork surface transformation **Angie Jones** — who led AI enablement across Block's 12,000 employees in the first half of 2025 before the CTO tasked her with building an agentic engineering org — recounts a paradox familiar to many technology leaders: by mid-2025, 90% of Block's 3,500 engineers were using tools like Goose and Claude Code, yet the CEO correctly observed that shipping velocity had not budged. This gap between adoption and impact — between token bills and shipped features — drove Jones to develop a staged maturity model for how engineers work with AI, a selective Champions program, and eventually an autonomous pipeline capable of taking a bug report from Slack to a PR in five minutes. The episode's closing twist — layoffs that followed this success — forces a reckoning with the question she poses outright: *"What are we doing? Where are we heading? And are we sure that it's where we want to end up?"* --- ## The Adoption-Impact Gap Jones describes a company that, by the numbers, looked like it had fully embraced AI. Internal coding agent Goose was built before LLMs supported tool calling; Block worked with Anthropic as design partners for the initial release of MCP, and Goose became the reference implementation for the MCP client. After a couple of months, roughly 90% of engineers were using Goose and Claude Code regularly. Yet the CEO was convinced engineering was not using AI at all — because nothing was shipping faster. > *"I had the numbers, both the metrics and the token bills. So I knew that engineering was in fact using AI, but he was right. Features certainly weren't making it to our customers any faster."* Jones frames AI enablement in three phases: **experimentation**, **adoption**, and **impact**. The org had surpassed experimentation and reached adoption (90% usage) but remained stuck there — engineers used AI inside the IDE to ask questions or write boilerplate, not to produce shippable work. The missing link was integrating AI into *how the team built and shipped*, not just how individual engineers coded. --- ## The Maturity Model and the 1-9-90 Strategy Jones created a five-stage model for an engineer's relationship with AI agents, later reorganized after reading Steve Yegge's "Gastown" article: | Stage | Behavior | |-------|----------| | 0 | Does not use AI tools in workflow | | 1 | Uses AI for auto-complete; never uses agent mode | | 2 | Chats with agents but does not use them to produce PRs | | 3 | Delegates tasks to agents and reviews the output | | 4 | Runs multiple agents in parallel | | 5 | Delegates complete tasks to agents; agents produce shippable results without human handholding | By mid-2025, most of Block's engineers sat between stages 1 and 2. Jones needed them at stage 5, but three obstacles blocked a top-down approach: (1) no playbook existed for any of this, (2) best practices became obsolete weekly, causing AI fatigue, and (3) engineers were already turned off by "AI or die" pressure from leadership. She applied the **1-9-90 rule** — in digital communities, 1% create, 9% interact, 90% passively consume. Rather than trying to level up all 3,500 engineers individually, she focused on forming the 1% from critical teams: an **AI Champions program** of 50 hand-picked engineers. > *"I realized that if my AI strategy depends on every individual leveling themselves up, I'm never going to see that broad impact."* Selection was strategic, not volunteer-based. Requirements: willingness to dedicate at least 30% of time to AI enablement, and resilience against the non-deterministic nature of AI. Jones spent a week talking to tech leads and managers to identify engineers from every corner of Block — Square, Cash App, Afterpay, Tidal — across frontend, backend, mobile, data, and infra, covering "the nasty big legacy, massive model repos, smaller services, mobile apps." --- ## Making Repos AI-Ready The first area of focus for the Champions was **repo AI-readiness**. Jones's theory: if engineers embed AI directly into repos, agents perform better and the entire team benefits — not just the 1%. Repos are a central point of reference for every engineer contributing code. The Champions added assets that became a standard set of components, customized by team: | Component | Purpose | |-----------|---------| | Context files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) | Provide repo guidance for the agent | | Rules files | Provide guardrails for agent behavior | | Repeatable workflows | Slash commands and later agent skills | | AI code reviewer (with instructions) | Review code on matters that matter to the team | | AI attribution on PRs | Tag which PRs are AI-authored | Different repo shapes required different approaches. Monorepos used shared context at the root with layered, specific rules at the service level — JVM developers were already strong in inheritance patterns, so this mapped naturally. What worked for web did not work for mobile; Android and iOS sometimes needed different approaches. Instead of a one-size-fits-all mandate, each champion figured out what worked for their repo, and teams with similar shapes converged on the same patterns — a bottom-up convergence rather than a top-down dictate. --- ## From Chat to Delegation Three months into the Champions program — around September 2025 — results were strong. AI-authored code was up **69%** , reported time savings increased **37%** , and automated PRs increased **21x**. But only the Champions had reached stage 3 (delegation); most engineers still operated at stages 1–2. Jones wanted delegation to feel native to how people already worked. The three natural channels for receiving requirements were **issue trackers** (Jira, Linear), **GitHub issues**, and **Slack**. The Champions implemented delegation from all three. The Slack flow became the most vivid illustration: > *"True story: we were in Slack one day, an engineer saw a bug with the product and wrote, 'Hey, I saw this bug, anybody else seen it?' Engineer two responds, 'No, I hadn't seen that one.' Engineer three calls Goose right there in Slack and says, 'Hey Goose, have you seen this bug before? Can you go and check if this is a bug?' Goose goes to the repo, pulls the file, says, 'Yep, this is a bug, here it is right here, but here's also three options of how you might implement a solution' — right there in Slack, code snippets. Engineer one says, 'I like option one.' Engineer two agrees. Engineer three says, 'Hey Goose, go implement option one.' Goose does so, returns with a link to the PR. The entire cycle from discussion, triage, diagnosis, issue creation, alignment, and the fix took like five minutes, all right there in Slack."* Engineers could also assign Linear tickets, Jira tickets, and GitHub issues directly to an agent, which would implement the work end-to-end. Agents became part of the sprint. In the first team to try this, the team ran out of work and had to pull in more tickets *twice*. The critical insight: all of this worked because the Champions had already laid the repo-readiness foundation. Engineers did not need to learn new skills — delegation was native to tools they already used. --- ## Multi-Agent Parallelism and the Bottlenecks Moving to stage 4 — running multiple agents in parallel — introduced two problems that had to be solved before stage 5 was reachable. **First, code review.** Engineers tripling or quadrupling their PR output overwhelmed human reviewers. The AI code reviewers that had been optional earlier in the process were initially hated — they "sucked so badly" that they pissed engineers off. But repo-readiness work, coupled with better models and tools (specifically **Codex**), made them viable. Jones enabled Codex on all repos and added an **auto-fix loop**: if Codex identified issues, another agent would automatically fix them and commit to the PR. By the time a human looked at a bot-written PR, it was in good shape. **Second, compute.** Running multiple agents simultaneously caused engineers' laptops to run out of memory and CPU. Block invested in dedicated **cloud workspaces** where each agent ran in its own isolated environment, enabling parallel execution from anywhere. --- ## BuilderBot, the World Model, and Stage 5 A small group of engineers — including many of the AI Champions — built an orchestrator called **BuilderBot** to coordinate agents. The key insight: to achieve anything close to autonomous engineering, agents needed to understand where everything lives and what depends on what. Block built a **company world model** based on the entirety of its **25,000-repo codebase** — a machine-readable view of every service and how they connect. This allowed orchestrators and their delegated agents to pull context as needed and understand the landscape during implementation. Multiple agents could explore different parts of the system in parallel, each building their own understanding, then come back together while the orchestrator assembled a plan spanning multiple codebases. This was especially useful for offerings that crossed Square, Cash App, Afterpay, and Tidal. With BuilderBot, Block reached stage 5: engineers delegating complete tasks to agents that produce shippable results without human handholding. Anyone at the company — not just engineers — could add BuilderBot in Slack and have it fix a bug or implement a new feature, without needing GitHub access at all. --- ## The Cost of Success > *"This felt like a dream. Until it became a nightmare."* Jones describes layoffs that happened the day before the episode (around June 27, 2026) as feeling different from previous rounds. She asks openly: *"Was this my fault? Did enabling employees to do the most incredible work of their careers ultimately result in their dismissal?"* The episode closes with three questions, left unanswered: > *"What are we doing? Where are we heading? And are we sure that it's where we want to end up?"* --- ## Cross-Theme Synthesis The episode presents a clear technical arc — from individual tool adoption to multi-agent orchestration — and an opaque human consequence. The technical playbook is detailed and replicable: start with a maturity model, select a 1% of champions, make repos AI-ready (context files, rules, code reviewers, cloud workspaces), then layer delegation channels and an orchestrator with a world model. The champion model is the key strategic innovation — it sidesteps the impossible task of leveling up 3,500 individuals simultaneously and instead lets infrastructure and patterns cascade. The unresolved tension is directional: Jones built what she was asked to build — an autonomous engineering org — but the episode never answers whether the org's autonomy or the resulting layoffs is the true outcome of the same trajectory. The closing questions are left hanging for a reason. For a finance or technology professional, the takeaway is twofold: the technical approach is concrete enough to adapt, and the ethical question — "to what end?" — is not an afterthought but the final signal of the episode. ai_security.title: ARMOR++: Agentic Orchestration of a Multi-Domain Primitive Set for Transferable Attacks on Deepfake Detectors
ai_security.abstract: The reliability of deepfake detectors frequently degrades under black-box adversarial transfer, as these models often rely on fragile, architecture-dependent forensic cues. Existing transfer attacks often lack semantic awareness and struggle to maintain effectiveness under strict no-query constraints, particularly when perturbations are transferred from convolutional surrogates to transformer-based targets. To address these limitations, this paper introduces ARMOR++, a robust multi-agent framework designed for high-transferability deepfake evasion. The framework leverages the Qwen2.5-VL Vision-Language Model (VLM) to supply spatial semantic priors, while the Qwen3 Large Language Model (LLM) orchestrates primitive selection, adaptive hyperparameter reparameterization, and entropy-regularized perturbation mixing. By integrating five complementary primitives, spanning dense optimization, saliency-based methods, spatial transformations, frequency-domain perturbations, and block-structured modifications, ARMOR++ effectively targets heterogeneous inductive biases. Rigorous evaluation on the AADD-2025 benchmark demonstrates that ARMOR++ significantly outperforms existing agentic and non-agentic baselines across both low- and high-quality image regimes. Statistical analysis confirms a substantial gain in blind-target Attack Success Rate (ASR) over the state-of-the-art agentic baseline, with further performance advantages evidenced against non-agentic benchmarks and under robust defensive configurations. These findings highlight a significant residual reliability gap in current deepfake detector deployments and demonstrate the efficacy of agentic orchestration in identifying latent vulnerabilities.

ai_security.title: Pretraining Data Can Be Poisoned through Computational Propaganda
ai_security.abstract: Poisoning pretraining data can introduce harmful behaviors to LMs that are difficult to detect and mitigate. Prior work on poisoning pretraining data has largely exploited established data sources such as Wikipedia, which do not represent the large scale and heterogeneity typical of pretraining corpora, and has ignored the interaction between poisoned data and data curation pipelines. We demonstrate that poisoning attacks on pretraining data are feasible beyond this limited setting through an existing web-scale content injection mechanism: public discussion interfaces. Additionally, to measure whether malicious content is included after web crawling and data curation, we introduce HalfLife, a novel analysis for estimating adversarial content inclusion in web-crawl based LM training data. We use HalfLife to explore the feasibility of poisoning pretraining corpora at web scale through open discussion interfaces. Our analysis demonstrates the importance of estimating whether poison injections are included in pretraining data, and establishes third-party webpage content as a possible vector for attacking language model pretraining.

ai_security.title: SciDiagramEdit: Learning to Edit Scientific Diagrams from Paper Revisions
ai_security.abstract: Editing the figures in a research paper is a routine and time-consuming part of everyday research practice: authors relabel components, rearrange panels, and restyle visuals as they revise their manuscripts. Automating this editing workflow under a natural-language instruction, however, is challenging, because a scientific figure is a dense infographic in which heterogeneous visual elements such as schematics, plots, photos, captions, and arrows are composed under a tight visual grammar to advance a specific argument. To address this, we present SciDiagramEdit, a benchmark and skill-evolution framework that learns from natural paper revisions and operates on the figure's editable vector source, where users can inspect and co-edit individual primitives alongside the agent. Our benchmark mines before/after figure pairs from arXiv version histories, each grounded in the authors' own revision intent. To accommodate the diversity of editing instructions, we adopt agentic learning via skill evolution: an agentic proposer continually refines the agent's skill specification from execution traces over multiple epochs. The resulting skill progressively lifts edit accuracy on a held-out validation set, providing evidence that natural paper revisions are an effective training signal for instruction-driven figure editing.
